Electrical discharge machining of nickel-based superalloys is sensitive to the tool electrode material because electrode properties strongly influence process efficiency, accuracy, and surface quality. Nowicki et al. report that graphite electrodes are increasingly adopted due to low cost, ease of machining, and high sublimation temperature, and that graphite grain size affects machining outcomes: coarser-grained graphite increased material removal rate but raised relative tool wear, while finer-grained graphite produced lower surface roughness. (Nowicki et al. 2022)

A more recent study by the same group refines this finding for Hastelloy C-22 and negative polarity EDM: using POCO AF-5 ($1\ \mu$m) and POCO EDM-180 ($10\ \mu$m) graphite electrodes, they found that fine-grained graphite improves process efficiency and reduces tool wear, and that detached graphite grains can destabilize discharges and thus influence removal mechanisms. (Nowicki et al. 2024) These experiments also produced predictive mathematical models relating electrode grain size and machining settings to MRR, relative TWR, and Ra. (Nowicki et al. 2024)

Across studies of high-performance alloys, electrical parameters dominate performance outcomes: peak current and pulse duration (or pulse-on time) repeatedly emerge as primary drivers of MRR and surface roughness. (Nowicki et al. 2022)(Nas & Kara 2022) In experiments on titanium and other alloys, amperage (peak current) accounted for the largest share of variance in MRR and TWR according to ANOVA analyses reported. (Akıncıoğlu 2022)

Electrode geometry and wear behaviour are also critical in practice: in EDM of Hastelloy B2, current and pulse duration strongly influence electrode taper, radius, wear length and cutting time, with sharp-edged square electrodes becoming hemispherical at the ends as a result of unstable sparks and heat diffusion. (Ramabalan et al. 2024) This illustrates how thermal and geometric transformations of the tool during EDM can undermine dimensional fidelity and increase effective electrode consumption. (Ramabalan et al. 2024)

To mitigate high TWR and low MRR inherent to EDM, several adjunct techniques are reported. Combining EDM with cryogenic treatments, powder-mixed dielectric, ultrasonic assistance, and similar methods has been investigated to improve MRR, reduce TWR, and refine surface integrity. (Shastri et al. 2022) Nanopowder-mixed EDM and cryogenically treated electrodes have been explored for other materials, where reported reductions in electrode wear and overcut were attributed to altered discharge behaviour and dielectric properties. (Sana et al. 2024) Separately, electrical discharge coating (EDC) is presented as a surface-modification variant that can deposit protective or functional layers via discharges, which may be relevant to managing surface integrity in EDM processes. (Liew et al. 2020)

Despite these findings, direct experimental comparisons of copper, graphite, and composite electrodes for Hastelloy alloys (quantifying TWR and MRR under controlled parameter sets) are not present in the cited literature. [[NEEDS SOURCE: Studies of composite electrode performance on Hastelloy]]
rows.b:
Nowicki et al. report that graphite electrodes with larger grain size produced higher process efficiency but also greater relative tool wear when machining Hastelloy C-22, and that the finest surface finish was achieved with the smaller-grain graphite AF-5. (Nowicki et al. 2022)

The same authors later found that fine-grained graphite increased material removal effectiveness and reduced tool wear in negative-polarity EDM of Hastelloy C-22, and they link detached graphite grains to reduced discharge stability and process efficiency. (Nowicki et al. 2024) These experiments used POCO AF-5 ($1\ \mu\text{m}$) and POCO EDM-180 ($10\ \mu\text{m}$) electrodes and produced empirical and mathematical models relating machining parameters to MRR, relative TWR and Ra. (Nowicki et al. 2022)(Nowicki et al. 2024)

Peak current and pulse duration emerge repeatedly as dominant drivers of MRR and surface roughness in nickel-based alloy EDM studies: Nowicki et al. identify discharge current and pulse duration as the principal factors controlling MRR and Ra for both graphite grades. (Nowicki et al. 2022) Nas & Kara quantify peak current as the single most influential factor for both MRR and Ra in their Taguchi-ANOVA analysis, attributing 86.43% of MRR variance and 74.79% of Ra variance to peak current in their experiments. (Nas & Kara 2022) Akıncıoğlu similarly reports amperage as the overwhelmingly dominant factor for MRR and TWR in Titanium EDM experiments, with ANOVA percentages above 99% for several responses. (Akıncıoğlu 2022) Together these studies indicate that current (amperage/peak current) and pulse-on time/pulse duration are the principal process parameters affecting MRR, TWR and Ra across non-conventional-machining studies cited here. (Nowicki et al. 2022)(Nas & Kara 2022)(Akıncıoğlu 2022)

For electrode wear specifically, Ramabalan et al. find that current and pulse duration strongly affect electrode shape loss and wear length when machining a Hastelloy variant, observing that sharp square-electrode edges are transformed to hemispherical ends under unstable sparking and heat diffusion. (Ramabalan et al. 2024) Shastri et al. summarise that high TWR, low MRR and coarse surface finish are common EDM challenges and list several process augmentations (cryogenic treatment, powder-mixed dielectrics, ultrasonic assistance) that researchers have used to address these issues. (Shastri et al. 2022) Sana et al. demonstrate that electrode treatments (cryogenic) and dielectric modifications can markedly reduce electrode wear and overcut in brass electrodes under their experimental conditions. (Sana et al. 2024)

rows.a:
Electrical discharge machining studies of nickel-based alloys emphasise the importance of electrode material properties for process efficiency, dimensional accuracy and surface finish. Nowicki et al. report that the choice of electrode material and its microstructure (specifically graphite grain size) strongly influences material removal rate (MRR), tool wear rate (TWR) and surface roughness (Ra) when machining Hastelloy C-22, and they derive empirical models relating machining parameters to these indicators. (Nowicki et al. 2022)

Two detailed experimental investigations of graphite electrodes on Hastelloy C-22 find consistent trends but add different emphases. Nowicki et al. (2024) show that finer-grained graphite increases process efficiency while reducing relative tool wear, and they attribute variations in discharge stability and process efficiency to detachment of graphite grains from the electrode. (Nowicki et al. 2024) Nowicki et al. (2022) also found that larger-grain graphite delivers higher MRR but with greater relative tool wear, whereas the finest-grain electrode produced the lowest Ra; both studies identify discharge current and pulse duration as primary drivers of MRR and Ra, with the inter-pulse time most influential for relative tool wear in graphite. (Nowicki et al. 2022)(Nowicki et al. 2024)

Work on process parameter sensitivity across other high-performance alloys reinforces the dominant role of peak current and pulse duration in controlling MRR, TWR and surface quality. Nas & Kara applied a full-factorial design and Taguchi gray relational analysis to a corrosion-resistant superalloy and found peak current to be the single most influential factor for both Ra and MRR, with optimal combinations involving cryogenic treatment, pulse-on time and current. (Nas & Kara 2022) Ramabalan et al. quantify the effect of current and pulse duration on electrode geometry changes during EDM of Hastelloy B2, observing that unstable sparks drive rapid edge rounding and wear that transform sharp square electrodes into hemispherical ends. (Ramabalan et al. 2024) Akıncıoğlu reports similarly high sensitivity of MRR and TWR to amperage in experiments on titanium, with amperage dominating ANOVA results for multiple performance measures. (Akıncıoğlu 2022)

Researchers also explore process modifications and alternative electrode or dielectric strategies to reduce TWR and improve accuracy. Reviews and comparative studies highlight powder-mixed EDM, cryogenic treatments and hybrid assistance methods as routes to alter MRR, TWR and surface integrity, and one experimental study using nanopowder and treated brass electrodes reports substantial reductions in electrode wear and overcut under specific dielectric and treatment conditions. (Shastri et al. 2022)(Sana et al. 2024) Liew et al. summarise electrical discharge coating approaches that modify surface functions via discharges, indicating broader interest in discharge-mediated surface engineering. (Liew et al. 2020)

Despite these contributions, direct comparative evidence on composite electrodes versus conventional copper or graphite electrodes specifically for Hastelloy alloys is not present in the surveyed material.
rows.b:
The experiments on Hastelloy C-22 found that graphite electrodes with larger grain size increased material removal rate while also producing higher relative tool wear, and that the finest surface finish came from the smaller-grain graphite; discharge current and pulse duration were identified as the principal controls on MRR and Ra, while the time interval (off-time) dominated relative graphite wear. (Nowicki et al. 2022)

A subsequent study that also machined Hastelloy C-22 with negative polarity corroborated that using fine-grained graphite raises process efficiency and lowers tool wear, and it further reported that graphite grains detaching from the electrode influence discharge stability and thereby the machining effectiveness; the authors translated their experimental results into predictive mathematical models relating electrode grain size and process settings to MRR, TWR and Ra. (Nowicki et al. 2024)

Work on a different Hastelloy variant (B2) emphasised the sensitivity of electrode geometry and wear to the thermal action of the sparks: higher current and longer pulse duration markedly increased electrode wear and rounded initially sharp electrode edges into hemispherical ends, with practical consequences for producing square holes where electrode wear changes hole geometry. (Ramabalan et al. 2024)

A factorial study that varied pulse-on time and peak current while comparing untreated and cryogenically treated superalloy samples showed that peak current dominated both surface roughness and material removal rate by large margins, and that an experimental combination with shallow cryogenic treatment, low peak current (6 A) and short pulse-on (300 μs) optimised the joint Ra–MRR objective according to Taguchi-gray relational analysis. (Nas & Kara 2022)

Reviews of EDM methods emphasise common process weaknesses (high tool wear, low MRR and elevated surface roughness) and summarise several intervention strategies that have been tested to mitigate these issues, including cryogenic electrode treatment, powder-mixed dielectric, ultrasonic assistance and other hybrid approaches. (Shastri et al. 2022) Experimental work using nanopowder-mixed dielectrics and cryogenically treated brass electrodes reported substantial reductions in electrode wear rate and improvements in dimensional accuracy for those electrode–dielectric combinations, demonstrating that electrode treatment and dielectric modification can strongly change EWR and overcut even where the electrode material differs from the workpiece. (Sana et al. 2024)

rows.a:
Selective Laser Melting (SLM) produces near-full-density metallic parts by layerwise melting and fusion of powder using a high power-density laser, a process that enables near net-shape components and has been applied across many metals. (Yap et al. 2015) The layerwise energy input and extreme local cooling in SLM create characteristic hierarchical microstructures with very fine subgrains and precipitates that differ from conventionally processed steels; these AM-specific features can enhance strength, wear resistance and corrosion resistance in some steels while posing challenges for ductility and fatigue. (Haghdadi et al. 2020) Evidence from MS300 produced by SLM shows that process choice also affects densification and porosity: SLM composites achieved higher densification and lower porosity than cold-sprayed counterparts, and such differences influence mechanical and surface-response properties. (Yan et al. 2018)

As-built SLM maraging steel typically exhibits a very fine martensitic microstructure produced by rapid solidification and cooling. (Tan et al. 2018) For example, SLM fabrication of grade 300 maraging steel produced submicron grain sizes consistent with cooling rates on the order of 10^7 K/s and a martensitic matrix containing needle-shaped Ni3X nanoprecipitates that contribute to age hardening. (Tan et al. 2018) Detailed EBSD work on SLM maraging steel reports a fine martensitic structure in multiple build-section orientations and, despite the layerwise build, no strong preferred texture was observed in one study. (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021)

Post-process heat treatments alter both the precipitation state and phase content, with consequences for mechanical and electrochemical behaviour. (Tan et al. 2018) Aging produces extensive precipitation that maximizes hardness and affects corrosion potential, whereas specific intercritical tempering can induce martensite-to-austenite reversion (reversed austenite) which concentrates Ni locally and nucleates along martensite lath boundaries. (Tan et al. 2018) Intercritical tempering that produced reversed austenite at ~720 °C led to improved pitting performance in 3.5 wt% NaCl: the tempered specimens with reversed austenite showed higher pitting potential, lower corrosion current density and lower corrosion rate than as-printed, aged, or homogenized samples without reversed austenite. (Khan et al. 2022)(Tan et al. 2018)

Surface condition and subsequent thermochemical or electrochemical surface treatments further influence corrosion behaviour. (Godec et al. 2021) Plasma nitriding applied to SLM 18Ni-300, when performed without prior aging, produced brittle cracks in the nitride compound layer, whereas nitriding after appropriate prior heat treatment improved wear and corrosion resistance relative to untreated SLM material. (Godec et al. 2021) Electropolishing significantly reduces the high as-printed surface roughness (Ra ≈ 10 µm) of SLM maraging steel and was shown to lower Ra by about 65%, with precipitation state controlling both nano-hardness and corrosion response in heat-treated conditions. (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021) Overall, studies agree that SLM-induced fine microstructure and precipitation strongly interact with heat treatment and surface finishes to determine corrosion performance in chloride environments. (Haghdadi et al. 2020)(Tan et al. 2018)
rows.b:
The as-built selective laser melting (SLM) maraging steel commonly presents an ultrafine martensitic matrix with submicron grains: an average grain size of 0.31 μm was reported and attributed to cooling rates on the order of $10^{7}\ \mathrm{K/s}$. (Tan et al. 2018) The same SLM condition produces a dense, near-full-density part when process parameters are optimised, which explains why studies treat the as-built microstructure as a fine, largely continuous martensitic network rather than a highly porous skeleton. (Yap et al. 2015) Electron-backscatter-diffraction mapping in three orthogonal sections showed a consistent fine martensitic structure across orientations in as-printed samples, with no pronounced crystallographic texture or anisotropy in the microstructure. (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021)

Aging and solution-type heat treatments alter both precipitate state and residual stress: large populations of needle-shaped Ni3X precipitates (X = Ti, Al, Mo) form within the martensitic matrix during appropriate ageing, and these precipitates are responsible for age hardening through mechanisms described as Orowan bowing and coherency strain. (Tan et al. 2018) Heat treatments also substantially relieve residual stresses induced by the layer-wise build and reduce, but do not entirely eliminate, the mechanical anisotropy associated with build orientation. (Tan et al. 2018) In comparative studies, heat-treated SLM maraging steel showed hardness and corrosion responses similar to conventionally processed equivalents when equivalent thermal cycles were applied, indicating that precipitation state largely controls these properties post-heat-treatment. (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021)

Intercritical tempering near the austenite-stability window produces reversed austenite that is spatially localised at martensite lath boundaries: tempering at about $720\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ generated reversed austenite precipitates primarily along lath boundaries, nucleated where local Ni enrichment followed dissolution of intermetallics. (Khan et al. 2022) That specific microstructural change correlated with electrochemical improvements measured in a chloride-containing electrolyte: the $720\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$-tempered specimens exhibited a higher pitting potential and a lower corrosion current density compared with as-printed, conventionally aged, and homogenised samples lacking reversed austenite. (Khan et al. 2022)

Thermo-chemical surface modification interacts with prior heat treatments: plasma nitriding carried out at $520\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ for 6 hours produced damaged nitride compound layers when applied without prior ageing, whereas performing nitriding after solution and aging treatments mitigated cracking and improved wear and corrosion resistance of the additive-manufactured material. (Godec et al. 2021) This indicates that the bulk precipitation and phase state prior to nitriding govern the integrity and protective function of the nitride layer. (Godec et al. 2021)

Surface condition and roughness remain key factors for corrosion behaviour in chloride environments: as-printed samples display a high surface roughness (Ra ≈ 10 μm), and electropolishing reduced Ra by about 65%, while ageing controlled precipitation and thereby influenced both hardness and corrosion potential. (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021) Taken together, the literature links three scales of microstructural control to chloride-induced corrosion performance in SLM maraging steel: nanoscale precipitate chemistry and distribution, mesoscale reversed-austenite formation at lath boundaries, and the macroscopic surface state shaped by as-built roughness and post-processing. (Tan et al. 2018)(Khan et al. 2022)(Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021)

Selective Laser Melting (SLM) creates near-full-density metal parts by layerwise melting and fusion of powder, producing components with up to 99.9% relative density when processing parameters are optimised. (Yap et al. 2015) This manufacturing route imposes very high cooling rates that produce a distinctive, very fine martensitic microstructure in grade 300 maraging steel: one study reports submicron grains with an average size of $0.31\ \mu$m and infers cooling on the order of $10^{7}\ \mathrm{K/s}$. (Tan et al. 2018) Electron microscopy in the same work identified abundant needle-shaped Ni$_3$X (X = Ti, Al, Mo) nanoprecipitates in the martensitic matrix that are directly implicated in age hardening. (Tan et al. 2018) Reviews of AM steels emphasise that these hierarchical subgrain structures and fine precipitates arise from the layerwise thermal cycles and act as an intrinsic heat treatment that can increase strength, wear resistance and corrosion resistance compared with conventionally produced counterparts. (Haghdadi et al. 2020)

Post-build heat treatments alter both mechanical and corrosion-related properties by changing precipitate state, residual stress and phase constitution. Systematic characterisation of as-built and heat-treated SLM maraging steel shows that ageing maximises hardness and relieves residual stress, while solution treatments and intercritical tempering can induce phase changes such as austenite reversion. (Tan et al. 2018)(Godec et al. 2021) Aging is also identified as the principal microstructural driver of both hardness and corrosion response: precipitation dominates the observed shifts in nano-hardness and in corrosion potential after heat treatment. (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021)

Austenite reversion produced by intercritical tempering near the $\alpha'+\gamma$ range modifies corrosion behaviour in chloride-containing solutions: specimens tempered at $720\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ developed reversed austenite concentrated along martensite lath boundaries, attributed to local Ni enrichment from intermetallic dissolution, and these specimens showed higher pitting potential and lower corrosion current density in $3.5\ \mathrm{wt\%}$ NaCl than as-printed, aged, or homogenised samples. (Khan et al. 2022) At the same time, thermochemical treatments interact with prior heat history: plasma nitriding applied without prior ageing produced cracking in the compound nitride layer, whereas nitriding following prior heat treatments improved wear and corrosion resistance of SLM 18Ni-300 compared with untreated AM material. (Godec et al. 2021)

Surface state and roughness from SLM also affect corrosion outcomes. As-printed maraging steel presents a fine martensitic structure with an Ra of about $10\ \mu$m, and electropolishing that reduces Ra by roughly 65% was shown to influence measured corrosion behaviour; after heat treatment the corrosion behaviour of SLM and wrought maraging steel converged in the reported comparisons. (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021) Broad reviews note that the many process parameters in SLM (building orientation, heat treatment, energy density, surface quality) complicate generalisation of fatigue and corrosion performance and leave gaps in comprehensive understanding. (Afkhami et al. 2019)(Haghdadi et al. 2020)

SLM can produce near–full-density maraging-steel parts, with reported relative densities up to 99.9%. (Yap et al. 2015) This near-full densification combines with the layerwise, high-energy melting and rapid solidification of SLM to produce extremely fine microstructures and in situ thermal cycles that generate hierarchical subgrains and precipitation phenomena not typically seen in conventionally made steels. (Haghdadi et al. 2020) In one detailed study of SLM 300-grade maraging steel, an average submicron grain size of $0.31\ \mu\text{m}$ was measured and cooling rates were estimated up to $10^{7}\ \text{K/s}$; needle-shaped Ni$_3$X precipitates (X = Ti, Al, Mo) were observed within a martensitic matrix and linked to age hardening. (Tan et al. 2018)

As-built SLM maraging steel has been described as a fine-grained martensitic structure with substantial surface roughness and little crystallographic texture across build sections. (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021) The same work quantified the as-printed surface roughness as about $Ra=10\ \mu\text{m}$ and reported that heat treatment changes both hardness and corrosion potential, with precipitation identified as the dominant influence on those properties. (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021) Heat treatments applied to SLM parts relieve residual stresses and modify mechanical anisotropy introduced by the layerwise build, while also altering precipitation and strengthening mechanisms observed in the as-fabricated condition. (Tan et al. 2018)

Intercritical heat treatment that produces reversed austenite has a measurable effect on chloride-induced pitting: tempering within the mixed martensite–austenite range at $720^\circ\text{C}$ caused reversed austenite to form mainly along martensite-lath boundaries, nucleated where Ni is locally enriched after dissolution of intermetallics, and this microstructural change increased pitting potential and reduced corrosion current density in 3.5 wt% NaCl. (Khan et al. 2022) While that study demonstrates improved pitting resistance when reversed austenite is present, the broader influence of martensite-to-austenite reversion on corrosion across different SLM conditions remains incompletely resolved. (Khan et al. 2022)

Thermo-chemical surface treatments and aging interact with prior heat treatments to affect corrosion behaviour: plasma nitriding applied without prior aging produced cracks in the nitride compound layer, whereas nitriding after appropriate solution and aging treatments improved wear and corrosion resistance relative to untreated SLM material and to conventionally produced counterparts subjected to the same treatments. (Godec et al. 2021) Aging in SLM maraging steel was reported to give the highest nano-hardness and the lowest corrosion potential among the tested conditions, and electropolishing can reduce the as-printed surface roughness by about 65%, which is relevant because surface finish influences corrosion performance. (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021)(Godec et al. 2021)

rows.a:
Deployment of household rooftop photovoltaic (PV) in India is framed by ambitious national targets and a policy environment that foregrounds renewables. India articulates a large-scale solar capacity goal that assigns a substantial share to grid-connected rooftop PV, and reviewers situate these targets within wider government strategies to expand renewable generation and attract investment. (Goel 2016)(J & Majid 2020)

Financial barriers (upfront cost, perceived lifetime returns, and financing flexibility) feature prominently in empirical studies. Survey evidence from Kerala identifies government subsidies as a primary motivator because they reduce the initial risk of adopting a novel technology, and low equipment prices and maintenance costs further strengthen the economic case for households. (Parsad et al. 2020) A multi-country household questionnaire found that higher purchase cost and perceived financial risk depress willingness to adopt, while mechanisms that spread payments or lower short-term expense improve uptake. (Tanveer et al. 2021) Nationally representative analysis from Uganda similarly shows that affordability determines the type of solar product taken and that flexible payment schemes increase access for income-constrained households, indicating that payment design matters as much as headline subsidies. (Aarakit et al. 2021)

Knowledge, technical concerns and awareness also constrain household decisions. Parsad et al. report that limited technical familiarity and gaps in knowledge act as significant inhibitors in their Kerala samples, and their modelling highlights these factors among the important predictors of investment choice. (Parsad et al. 2020) Local pilot-project evaluation in Puducherry collected consumer responses about space availability, experience with rooftop systems, and usage patterns, underscoring that practical installation knowledge and household-level constraints (roof space, prior exposure) affect willingness to participate in rooftop programs. (Kappagantu et al. 2015) Cross‑sectional evidence from Pakistan similarly links perceived risks and self-efficacy to willingness to adopt, suggesting that perceived technical or operational risk reduces uptake until users feel competent or supported. (Tanveer et al. 2021)

Institutional and equity-related barriers appear across qualitative and mixed-methods work. Research synthesizing interviews, site visits and literature highlights that rapid solar deployment can create demographic and spatial inequities, and it calls attention to how supply chains, business models and policy design can exacerbate or mitigate injustices. (Sovacool et al. 2022) Case studies and reviews that document national policy ambitions also note implementation challenges and institutional frictions that complicate translating targets into equitable household adoption. (Goel 2016)(J & Majid 2020)
rows.b:
A multi-city survey of Pakistani households measured that higher perceived system cost reduces willingness to adopt rooftop PV, while social norms and self-efficacy increase it, indicating that price barriers and subjective beliefs act in opposite directions on household decisions. (Tanveer et al. 2021) Complementing this, nationally representative analysis from Uganda shows that affordability determines the kind of solar product households select and that offering flexible payment arrangements raises uptake among income-constrained rural households, implying that liquidity and payment terms can substitute for upfront affordability constraints. (Aarakit et al. 2021)

A field evaluation of a smart-grid pilot in Puducherry reported practical implementation barriers gathered from consumers, including questions about available roof space and user experience with rooftop systems, which indicates that site-specific physical constraints and user familiarity shape the feasibility of installations at the household level. (Kappagantu et al. 2015) This finding echoes the Kerala study’s identification of technical barriers as a significant inhibitor of investment, suggesting that both physical installation constraints and technical knowledge gaps reduce adoption likelihood. (Parsad et al. 2020)
